Because they don't share a common language, they start to create a "bridge" language. They take words from the strongest language in the area (the "superstrate") but simplify the grammar and pronunciation so everyone can understand. This process is called **creolization**.

When a language is created this way, it is built on **communication first, rules second.** In traditional languages like English or French, the spelling was often decided by kings, scholars, and printers hundreds of years ago. They kept old spellings even when the way people actually spoke changed. 

Creole languages, however, often develop in environments where there isn't a long history of formal "grammar books" or "dictionary makers" from the very beginning. Because the priority is making sure the message gets across, the way people speak is the "truth." 

When people eventually start writing these languages down, they often choose to write exactly what they hear. If the spoken word is the most important thing, then the spelling should match the sound perfectly. This is called **phonetic spelling**. It’s like drawing a picture of a dog: if your goal is to show someone what a dog looks like, you draw what you see. In creoles, the goal is to show what the word sounds like, so the spelling follows the sound!

Think of your house or your land like a big toy that you get to keep in your neighborhood. Even though you own it, you are using the neighborhood's shared space to keep your toy there. Because you are using that space, you have to pay a small "membership fee" every year. This fee is called property tax.

Why does the government need this money? They use it to pay for things that everyone in the neighborhood uses, but no single person could build or fix by themselves. Imagine if you wanted to build a giant playground, a big swimming pool, and a library all at once—it would be very expensive!

The government uses your property taxes to pay for:

1.  **Schools:** So kids have a place to learn and teachers have books.
2.  **Roads:** So cars and bikes can travel safely from one place to another.
3.  **Firefighters and Police:** So there are people ready to help if there is an emergency.
4.  **Parks:** So everyone has a nice place to run around and play.

Because these things help make your neighborhood a safe and happy place to live, the government asks everyone who owns property to chip in a little bit of money each year. It is like a group project: everyone pays a little so that everyone gets to enjoy a lot!

A straw man fallacy happens when someone ignores your actual argument and replaces it with a fake, exaggerated, or distorted version of what you said. It is much easier to "knock down" a fake version of an argument than it is to deal with your real point.

Imagine you are building a house out of bricks. A straw man fallacy is like someone pretending you are building a house out of wet tissue paper. Because tissue paper is weak and easy to destroy, they can "win" the argument by knocking it over, even though that wasn't what you were doing at all. They aren't attacking your real house; they are attacking a "straw man" they built to make you look wrong.

To make it even simpler, think of it as **misrepresenting someone's words to make them sound silly.**

**Here is a simple example:**

*   **Person A:** "I think we should spend less money on candy and more money on vegetables."
*   **Person B:** "So, what you’re saying is that you want to ban all sweets forever and make every child miserable? That is a terrible idea!"

In this scenario, Person A never said they wanted to ban sweets or make children miserable. They only suggested spending less on candy. However, Person B created a "straw man"—the idea of a total ban—because it is much easier to argue against "banning all sweets" than it is to argue against "buying fewer sweets."

By attacking the fake version of the argument, Person B avoids having to talk about the actual topic. Whenever you see someone say, "Oh, so what you're saying is [something extreme/ridiculous]," they are likely using a straw man fallacy.

Think of Germany like a big neighborhood and Prussia like a very powerful, wealthy family that lived in one of the houses.

Before the 1870s, "Germany" wasn't one single country. Instead, it was a collection of many different small countries (called states), like neighbors sharing a fence. Some were big, and some were tiny. They spoke the same language and shared a culture, but they each had their own rules and leaders.

Prussia was the biggest and strongest of these "neighboring" countries. Because Prussia had a huge army and a lot of land, it acted like the "big brother" of the neighborhood. While the other countries were smaller, Prussia was very organized and focused on becoming the most powerful.

Eventually, the big brother (Prussia) decided that instead of everyone living separately, they should all join together to form one giant country. They did this to become stronger against other neighbors. In 1871, Prussia led the way in uniting all those smaller states to create the modern nation of **Germany**.

So, to answer your question: Prussia was a kingdom that existed *before* the unified country of Germany was finished. Once Germany was formed, Prussia was still a part of it (the biggest part!), but it eventually lost its special status as a separate kingdom as Germany became one unified nation. 

In short: Prussia was the "leader" state that helped build the "house" we now call Germany.

To explain this simply, imagine you want to throw a huge birthday party, but there are several reasons why people might be upset about where you chose to hold it.

First, there is the **weather**. Qatar is extremely hot. For many people, football is a sport played outdoors in the grass. Because it was so hot in Qatar, the games had to be played at night under big stadium lights. This changed the "feeling" of the tournament for many fans who prefer a daytime atmosphere.

Second, there is the **environment**. Building massive stadiums, new airports, and entire cities takes a huge amount of energy and resources. Critics argue that it is not "green" or kind to the planet to build so much new stuff just for a sports event that only lasts one month.

Third, there are **human rights** concerns. This is the most serious part. To build those stadiums and roads, many people from other countries were brought in to do the hard work. Many reports showed that these workers were treated unfairly, paid very little, and lived in poor conditions. People feel it is wrong for a sports company to profit from people being treated poorly.

Finally, there is the **money**. The World Cup costs billions of dollars. Some people believe that money should be spent on things like schools, hospitals, or helping poor countries instead of building giant stadiums in a wealthy country.

In short, while the football matches were exciting, many people felt the "cost" of the party—to the planet, to the workers, and to the world's values—was too high.

Imagine you have a big jar of cookies. If you only have one cookie, you might need to give away a tiny crumb to help your friends. But if you have a thousand cookies, you have plenty to keep for yourself, so you can give away a few more cookies to help the community without going hungry.

Tax brackets work like this. Instead of everyone giving away the exact same percentage of their cookies, the rules change based on how many cookies you have. People who have very few cookies pay a small "crumb" because they need those cookies to stay full. People who have a mountain of cookies pay a bigger "slice" because they have more than they could ever eat alone.

You asked why we don't just have a "flat tax," where everyone gives away the exact same percentage (like 10%) no matter how many cookies they have. 

The reason we have brackets is to make things "fairer." If we had a flat tax of 20%, it might be very hard for someone who only makes a little money to pay it, because they need every penny for basic things like food and clothes. However, for someone who is very wealthy, 20% might feel like a tiny amount because they still have a huge pile of money left over.

By using brackets, the government tries to balance two things: making sure everyone can afford to live, and making sure that those who have "extra" help pay a bit more to build things like schools, roads, and parks that everyone uses. It’s like a team rule: the people with the biggest backpacks carry a little more weight so that the people with small backpacks can keep up with the group.

Imagine the air is like a giant shared room that everyone breathes in. To understand why China has more pollution than America, we have to look at two main things: how many people are in the room and what they are doing inside it.

First, you are right about the population. China has a huge number of people—more than double the population of America. Because there are so many people, there are many more factories, more cars on the roads, and more buildings being constructed. Think of it like a kitchen: if one person is cooking, there isn't much smoke. But if a hundred people are all cooking big meals at the same time, the room will get very smoky very fast.

Second, it is about *how* they are making things. For a long time, China grew very quickly by using "dirty" energy, like burning coal. Coal is like a campfire that produces lots of black soot; it’s cheap and easy to use, but it makes the air dirty. America has had more time to switch to "cleaner" ways of making power, like using wind, sun, or natural gas, which don't put as much smoke into the air.

So, the reason for the pollution is a mix of "too many people" and "using older, dirtier tools." Because China is still building many new things for its huge population, it creates a lot of smoke. However, China is now trying to change this by building more solar panels and electric cars to help clear the air, just like how we try to keep our own rooms clean!

Imagine your skin is like a thin piece of fabric. The skin under your eyes is the thinnest and most delicate part of your whole face. Because it is so thin, it acts like a window, letting you see what is happening underneath.

There are three main reasons why these "shadows" appear:

First, think about your blood vessels. Everyone has tiny tubes under their skin that carry blood. Because the skin under your eyes is so thin, those tubes show through more easily. When blood sits in those tubes, it looks like a bluish or purplish shadow. It’s like looking at a faint bruise through a piece of tissue paper.

Second, think about your "stuff." Sometimes, the skin under your eyes can get a little bit of extra pigment, which is like a tiny bit of extra paint. This can happen because of your family’s genes—some people are just born with a little extra "paint" in that spot.

Third, think about your habits. If you don't get enough sleep, your body gets tired, and the blood vessels can swell a little bit. Also, if you rub your eyes a lot, you might irritate the skin. When skin gets irritated or rubbed, it can get thicker or darker over time.

So, your dark rings aren't usually a scary problem! They are usually just a mix of your skin being very thin, your blood vessels showing through, and sometimes just a sign that your body needs a little extra rest.

Think of a prison sentence like a "score" for how bad a crime was. When a judge gives someone a sentence, they aren't just looking at how many years a person can physically live; they are looking at the seriousness of what the person did.

Imagine if a child broke a toy. A parent might say, "You are grounded for a week." Even if the child is only five years old, the "week" represents the punishment for the action. If the child did something much worse, the parent might say, "You are grounded until you are 100 years old!" The parent knows the child won't actually be 100, but the point is to show that the punishment is very, very big because the mistake was very, very big.

In the legal world, giving someone "Life in Prison" means they stay in jail until they die. However, some crimes are so terrible that the government wants to make sure the person can *never* leave, even if the laws change in the future. 

If a judge gives a person 200 years, it is a way of saying, "Your crime was so bad that you deserve the maximum punishment possible." It ensures that even if the person gets out of prison early due to a technicality or a change in the law, they still have a huge amount of time left to serve. It is a way to show that the crime is permanent and the punishment is meant to last for the rest of their life, plus more. It is about the weight of the crime, not the calendar of a human life.

To understand how political parties switched "sides," it helps to think of them like sports teams. The teams stay the same, but the players and the rules of the game change over time.

In the 1850s, the parties were almost opposites regarding slavery. The Republicans were the "new" team formed to stop slavery from spreading, while the Democrats were the "old" team that mostly supported it. Today, the roles are flipped: Democrats are the party that opposes slavery (and other systems of oppression), while Republicans are the party that generally favors more conservative traditions.

So, when did the switch happen? There wasn't one single day when everyone jumped across the street. Instead, it was a slow "drift" that took about 100 years.

First, during the late 1800s, the parties began to focus more on money and factories. The Republicans became the party of big business and high taxes, while Democrats became the party of farmers and small government.

Then, during the 1930s, a huge shift happened called the "New Deal." President Franklin D. Roosevelt (a Democrat) started the government spending a lot of money to help people during the Great Depression. This made many people who liked "big government" start joining the Democratic Party.

Finally, in the 1960s, the parties shifted on social issues like civil rights. Democrats became the home for people who wanted rapid social change, while Republicans became the home for people who wanted to keep things the way they were.

By the time we get to today, the "labels" have moved. The Republican Party now holds many of the views that the old Democrats held, and the Democratic Party holds the views that the old Republicans held. It is like the teams kept their names, but they traded their jerseys and playbooks.

To understand the difference between a cult and a religion, you have to look at the "rules" and the "vibe," not the number of people in the group. Imagine two different clubs.

If a group of three people meets in a basement to pray together, and a group of three million people meets in a stadium to pray together, the size doesn't change what they are doing. If both groups believe in the same gods, follow the same holy books, and have been around for hundreds of years, they are both religions.

Think of it like a "fan club." If you have a tiny fan club for a superhero, it’s still a fan club. If you have a massive fan club for that same superhero, it’s still a fan club. The size doesn't change the *type* of club it is.

So, how do we tell them apart? It is usually about three things:

First, **Time.** Religions are usually very old. They have survived for centuries, passed down through grandparents and great-grandparents. Cults are often "new" and started by one specific person very recently.

Second, **Control.** In a cult, the leader usually has total power over your life. They might tell you who to marry, what to eat, and who you can talk to. In a religion, while there are leaders, you usually have more freedom to make your own choices.

Third, **The Goal.** Religions usually try to help people be better humans or connect with a higher power. Cults often focus on making the leader rich, powerful, or famous.

In short: Size doesn't matter. A religion is a long-lasting community with shared beliefs, while a cult is often a new group where one leader has too much control over everyone else.

Imagine you are riding your bike. If you want to go fast, you lean forward and make yourself "slippery" so the wind slides past you. That is aerodynamics! However, city buses aren't trying to win a race; they are trying to be big, safe, and useful.

There are three main reasons why they are shaped like big boxes.

First, think about what needs to fit inside. A bus is like a giant moving room. To fit as many people as possible, you want a wide, rectangular space. If the front were pointy like a rocket, the inside would get narrower and narrower, making it hard for people to sit or for the driver to see. A flat front gives the bus the most "room" for its passengers.

Second, it is about safety. A flat, wide front acts like a shield. If a bus has a very pointy nose, it might be harder for the driver to see exactly what is right in front of them. A flat front provides a clear "window" of vision and a sturdy wall that protects everyone inside.

Finally, there is the "speed" secret. Even though a bus looks like a brick, it doesn't actually go very fast. Most city buses drive slowly in traffic. Because they aren't moving at high speeds, the amount of air pushing against the front isn't a huge problem. The money the city saves by making the bus a simple square shape is much higher than the tiny amount of gas they would save by making it curvy. 

In short, buses are shaped like boxes because they prioritize **space, safety, and cost** over being fast!

Think of your ears like tiny, high-tech microphones. These microphones are connected to your brain by long wires called nerves. These nerves are constantly sending messages to your brain, telling it about every sound around you, even the tiny ones you don't notice.

Sometimes, these nerves get a little "confused" or "hyper." Imagine if you were trying to sleep and a tiny spark of static electricity jumped across a wire. That is what happens inside your head. For a few seconds, a nerve sends a fake "loud" signal to your brain. Because the signal is so fast and sharp, your brain interprets it as a high-pitched whistle or a beep.

This happens because your ears are always "on." Even when it is quiet, your ears are working hard to listen. Occasionally, a tiny muscle in your ear might twitch, or a tiny bit of fluid might move, or a nerve might just have a "hiccup." It is like a tiny glitch in a computer game; the game keeps running perfectly, but for one second, a weird sound pops up and then disappears.

Since it only lasts a few seconds and then goes away, it usually means your ears are just being very sensitive. Your brain is doing its job of listening so well that it sometimes catches a tiny "glitch" from your own nervous system. It isn't a permanent problem; it is just your body's internal electronics having a very brief, noisy moment!

Imagine your computer is like a big playroom filled with toys. Each file on your computer is like a toy.

When you move a file to the **Recycle Bin**, it is like taking a toy off the shelf and putting it into a big toy box in the corner of the room. The toy isn't gone forever; it is just tucked away inside the box. You can still see the box, and if you change your mind, you can open the lid, grab the toy, and put it back on the shelf. It is still taking up space in your room, it’s just hidden away so you don't have to look at it anymore.

When you **clear the Recycle Bin completely**, it is like taking all those toys out of the box and giving them away to a giant warehouse far, far away. Once you do this, the toys are no longer in your room, and you can't just reach into the box to get them back. 

**Where do the files go?** 
Technically, they don't actually travel to a different place immediately. On your computer’s "hard drive," the space where those toys were sitting gets marked as "empty." It’s like erasing the name of a toy from a list. The computer now thinks that spot is available for new toys. Until you put something new in that exact spot, the old information stays there as "ghost" data, but the computer won't let you see it or use it anymore. Eventually, when you save new files, the computer will write over those old "ghosts," and then they are gone for good!

To understand why two negatives make a positive, it helps to stop thinking about numbers as just "amounts" and start thinking about them as **directions** and **actions**.

Imagine you are standing on a giant number line. You are currently at zero. In this world, we have two types of actions:
1.  **Walking forward** is a positive action (+).
2.  **Walking backward** is a negative action (-).

We also have two types of numbers:
1.  **Positive numbers** mean "facing East" (the right side).
2.  **Negative numbers** mean "facing West" (the left side).

Multiplication is simply a set of instructions: **(Direction you are facing) × (Action you take).**

If you multiply $3 \times 2$, it means: Face East (positive) and walk forward 3 steps, twice. You end up at $+6$.

If you multiply $3 \times (-2)$, it means: Face East (positive) and walk backward 2 steps, three times. You end up at $-6$.

Now, here is the magic part. What happens when you multiply $-3 \times -2$?
The first negative sign ($-3$) tells you to **face West**.
The second negative sign ($-2$) tells you to **walk backward** 2 steps, three times.

If you are facing West and you walk backward, which way are you actually moving? You are moving toward the East! Because you flipped your direction twice (once by facing the wrong way and once by walking the wrong way), you end up moving in the positive direction. You land on $+6$.

In mathematics, this is called the **Distributive Property**. If we want $(-1) \times (-1)$ to make sense, it has to equal $1$ to keep all other math rules consistent. If it equaled $-1$, the entire logic of algebra would break, and we wouldn't be able to solve basic equations!

Not everything has a melting or boiling point in the way you might think. To understand why, we have to look at how things are built.

Imagine you have a big box of LEGO bricks. If the bricks are just sitting there, you can move them around easily. This is like a **liquid**. If you snap them all together into a solid tower, they stay put. This is like a **solid**. To turn the tower into a liquid, you need to add energy (heat) to break those snaps. That "breaking point" is the **melting point**.

Most simple things, like ice, water, or gold, are made of tiny "bricks" (atoms or molecules) that are held together by simple snaps. When you heat them up enough, the snaps break, and they melt or boil.

However, some things are not made of simple bricks. **Wood** is a "complex" material. It is made of long, tangled chains of fibers (called cellulose), mixed with water, air, and resins. It’s more like a giant, messy ball of yarn than a neat tower of LEGOs.

Because wood is so complex, it doesn't have one single melting point. If you heat wood, the water inside turns to steam first. Then, the chemicals inside start to break down and turn into gas or charcoal. Instead of melting into a puddle like an ice cube, wood **decomposes** or burns. It falls apart piece by piece rather than changing states all at once.

So, while simple substances have clear melting points, complex things like wood, plastic, or even your body don't "melt" in the traditional sense—they break down!

Think of your heart like a pump that moves water through a garden hose. If you have a bucket of water and you pour it out very slowly, it lasts a long time. If you pour it out very fast, the bucket empties quickly. 

Your heart has a "budget" of about a billion beats. If you lived a very lazy life and never moved, your heart would beat slowly and steadily, potentially lasting a long time. However, if you were constantly stressed or sedentary, your heart might work inefficiently, wearing out sooner than it should.

So, why do we exercise? Cardio exercise is like "strength training" for your pump. When you run or swim, you are asking your heart to move more blood than usual. This makes the heart muscle get bigger and stronger—just like your biceps. A stronger heart doesn't have to work as hard to move the same amount of blood. It becomes more efficient. Instead of "spending" your heartbeats quickly, a strong heart uses them wisely. It can pump more blood with every single beat, which actually helps your heart last longer and stay healthy.

Is it the same as other muscles? Yes and no. When you lift weights, your biceps get bigger to handle heavy loads. When you do cardio, your heart gets stronger to handle "volume" (moving lots of blood). 

In short: Exercise doesn't give you "extra" beats in your lifetime budget. Instead, it trains your heart to be a high-quality pump. A strong pump doesn't get tired as easily and can do its job much better, making your body run smoothly for as long as possible.

Think of a photo like a **painting** and a video like a **flipbook**.

When you take a photo, you are capturing one single moment in time. Because it is just one still image, your camera can use a massive amount of detail to make it look perfect. Imagine a giant mosaic made of millions of tiny tiles. If you look at it closely, you can see every single tile clearly. That is what a high-megapixel photo is—a huge amount of data packed into one "frozen" frame.

Now, think about a video. A video isn't just one image; it is a fast series of images shown one after another. To make a video look smooth, your camera has to "paint" those pictures very, very fast—usually 30 or 60 pictures every single second!

If your camera tried to record 4K video at 4 megapixels, it would be like trying to draw 60 beautiful, detailed paintings every second by hand. You would run out of "ink" and "time" almost instantly! 

There are three main reasons why video resolution stays lower than photo resolution:

1.  **Processing Power:** Your phone or camera has a brain (a processor). If it had to calculate billions of pixels 60 times a second, the device would get incredibly hot and the video would stutter or freeze.
2.  **Storage Space:** A high-megapixel video would take up so much room that you could only record a few seconds before your memory was full.
3.  **Internet Speed:** Streaming a 100-megapixel video would be impossible because your internet isn't fast enough to send that much data to your screen.

In short, photos are about **depth**, while videos are about **speed**. We sacrifice some detail in video so that the motion can stay smooth and the files can actually be played!

It might seem strange to give away your "secret recipes" for free, but for companies like Tesla and Toyota, this is a very smart long-term strategy. Think of it like a playground: if you want everyone to play a new game with you, it is much better if everyone knows the rules.

First, these companies want to create a "standard." If Tesla shares its battery or charging technology, they want every other car company to use their specific system. If everyone uses the same "plug" or "language," it makes it much easier for Tesla to dominate the market because their technology becomes the foundation for everyone else. It is easier to be the leader of a huge group than to be the only person playing a game no one else knows how to join.

Second, it helps the industry grow faster. Electric vehicles (EVs) are still relatively new. If every company spends years trying to reinvent the wheel individually, it takes a long time for people to start buying these cars. By sharing patents, companies help the entire industry move forward quickly. When more people buy EVs, the factories get bigger, the costs go down, and the technology improves for everyone. This creates a massive market that benefits everyone, including the companies that shared the secrets.

Finally, it builds a "good guy" reputation. By being open, these companies position themselves as leaders of a movement rather than just competitors. It makes it harder for smaller companies to complain about "monopolies" if the big players are being generous. In short, they aren't giving away their secrets because they don't care about profit; they are giving them away to make sure their secrets become the world's standard.

Think of a **scientific law** as a "rulebook" for how nature behaves. It is a description of *what* happens every single time under certain conditions. For example, the law of gravity tells us that if you drop a ball, it will fall down. It doesn't explain why gravity exists; it just tells us exactly what will happen. It is like a shortcut: if you see "A" happen, you can be 100% sure that "B" will follow.

To understand the difference between a law and a theory, imagine you are trying to understand how a bicycle works.

A **Law** is the observation: "When I push the pedals, the wheels turn." It is a consistent, repeatable fact. It is the "what."

A **Theory** is the explanation: "The chain connects the pedals to the gears, which rotate the axle." A theory explains the "why" and the "how." It connects all the different pieces of information together to give us a big picture.

You mentioned that a theory is a hypothesis that hasn't been proven wrong. While that is partly true, there is a big difference in their jobs. A theory is never "promoted" to a law. They are two different tools in a scientist's toolbox. A law describes a pattern (like a rule in a game), while a theory explains the mechanics behind that pattern (like the instructions on how the game was built).

In short: A **Law** tells you what will happen (the pattern), and a **Theory** explains why it happens (the reason). Both are essential because, without laws, we wouldn't know what to expect, and without theories, we wouldn't understand the world around us.

When a person feels so sad or overwhelmed that they want to hurt themselves, they go to the hospital to get help from "heart doctors" for the mind, called psychiatrists and counselors. The hospital is a safe place where the main goal is to keep the person safe and help them feel better.

First, the doctors talk to the person. They ask questions to understand why the person feels this way and what is making them sad. They want to listen to the person's story so they can figure out how to help.

Next, the hospital makes sure the person is safe. This means they might keep the person in a special room where there are no sharp objects, ropes, or anything else that could be used to cause harm. This is like a "safety zone" where the person can rest without any danger.

To treat the patient, doctors use different tools. Sometimes they give medicine that helps the brain feel calmer or happier. Other times, they use "talk therapy." This is when a kind person sits with the patient and teaches them how to handle big feelings, how to breathe through stress, and how to find hope again.

To make sure the person stays safe after they leave the hospital, the doctors create a "safety plan." This is like a map for the future. It lists things the person can do when they feel sad, like calling a special friend, going for a walk, or talking to a helper. They also make sure the person has regular "check-ups" to keep talking about their feelings. The goal isn't to punish the person; it is to surround them with love, medicine, and support until they feel strong enough to face the world again.

Imagine that everything in the world is made of tiny, tiny pieces called molecules. Water is made of molecules that love to move around and dance. When you spill water on your floor, these molecules are all huddled together in a big puddle.

However, there is something invisible in the air all around you called heat. Even if the room feels cool, there is enough heat energy to make the water molecules start wiggling. As they wiggle faster and faster, they get very excited! They start to jump around so much that they break away from their friends in the puddle.

This is called **evaporation**. 

Think of it like a group of kids at a playground. If they are all sitting together, they form a group. But if they all suddenly get a burst of energy and start running in different directions, the group disappears. The water molecules do the same thing. They turn into a gas called water vapor. Because gas is invisible, it blends right into the air.

So, the water didn't actually vanish into nothingness; it just changed its "outfit." It went from a liquid you can see into a gas you can’t see. It traveled into the air, floating around the room until it eventually finds a way to turn back into liquid again, like when it forms a cloud in the sky or a drop of dew on a leaf. Your floor is dry because the water molecules decided to go on an adventure into the air!
